title: Two rams in one field
hookLine: two rams lock horns: yesterday's effort and today's
carry: fate is past effort; today's effort pushes back
tomorrow: four guards stand at one gate. which one do you befriend first?
last: AN HONEST QUESTION IS A DOOR.

cards: Birth charts, fortune cookies, the 'it was meant to be' at the end of a wedding toast: the idea that a life is already written turns up everywhere.
Rama has just told the court that the world's prizes come and go on their own. A teacher could leave him there, with everything out of his hands. Vasistha doesn't.
He draws a picture instead: two rams with their horns locked in a field, and the stronger one pushing the other back.

teach.b: The Sanskrit words are paurusha, a person's own effort, and daiva, fate. Vasistha's move is bold. What people call fate, he says, isn't a separate power writing the story from outside.
It's the fruit of a person's own earlier effort, coming back around.

So when a life feels fixed, that's yesterday's effort pushing. Today's effort is the other ram, and the stronger one wins the field. The effort he praises isn't raw willpower; it's guided by scripture and good teachers.
A Christian neighbor would recognize part of this.

teach.h: PAUL: WHAT YOU SOW, YOU REAP.
teach.b: Paul writes to the Galatians: 'whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.' What you do comes back to you. That much the two share.
The honest difference is in the field itself. For Paul, the sowing happens before God, and the harvest he hopes for is life everlasting, reaped from the Spirit.
For Vasistha, fate is a person's own past actions, and present effort can overcome them.
Both say what you do matters. They say it inside two different pictures of the world. Vasistha's point to Rama is plain: sitting still and waiting on fate gets nothing done.

how: Hindu teachers who draw on the Yoga Vasistha often cite its chapters on effort when someone leans on fate; Christians hear Galatians 6:7 read as a call to live with care.

s: the Yoga Vasistha says your life is already written
Vasistha calls fate the fruit of past effort, and says today's effort can push it back.
Vasistha calls fate the fruit of a person's own past effort
not a separate power writing the story from outside.
Paul's 'whatsoever a man soweth' and Vasistha's teaching are the same idea
they share sowing and reaping; Paul speaks of God and life everlasting, Vasistha of one's own past effort.

games.q: your team lost its first three games, and the captain says the season is cursed. by Vasistha's two rams, what's the move?
o: treat the losses as last week's push, and out-train them now.
accept the curse; some seasons are just written that way.
blame the referees; fate is really other people's choices.
games.why: for Vasistha, what looks like fate is yesterday's effort pushing. today's effort is the other ram, and the stronger one wins the field.

practice: Plant both feet flat on the floor and press your palms together in front of your chest, gently, so each hand pushes against the other. Feel the two pushes meet and hold.
Then soften the pressure, keep your feet planted, and breathe with that steady, ready feeling.

wordCard.voice: The Yoga Vasistha: here, paurusha against daiva, today's effort against yesterday's, two rams in one field.

orig.note: Sanskrit paurusha: a person's own effort; in Vasistha's argument, the answer to daiva, fate.

carryVoice: For the road: fate is yesterday's effort, and today's effort can push back. Day sixteen-oh-two.
